name: threepenny-crook-pit-band
idea: A 1928 Berlin crook-cabaret pit band in the Threepenny manner, not piano-led: a chugging banjo and a wheezing harmonium carry the hustle, a nasal alto saxophone is the lead voice that sidles round the two envelopes, and a muted trumpet answers it sarcastically. Foley sits inside the band: a paper flick as the envelopes fan, a coin set on a wooden counter, a timpani thud landing on the switch at 7 s. At 10.5 s the band cuts out mid-phrase, leaving a single held harmonium chord and one dry banjo pluck as the curtain goes back, sparse enough for a line over it. Instrumental, a sour minor-key march-foxtrot, the sound of respectable people cheating.

name: hot-club-string-hustle
idea: A 1930s Paris string band with no piano and no drums: two acoustic rhythm guitars chop la pompe, an upright bass walks, and a swinging violin is the lead voice, smooth and playful, like the dealer's patter. On the pick (3.5-7 s) the violin dithers between two notes; on the switch it snaps into a sharp pizzicato pluck and a fast downward slide while the guitars stop dead. The last 4.5 s are almost empty: a bowed bass harmonic, one high violin harmonic held, and a faint rustle of banknotes. Acoustic, close-miked, warm and slightly crackly, instrumental only.

name: habanera-bandoneon-card-sharp
idea: A slinky 1930s tango duet: a parlour piano plays a sly habanera bass (the dotted, limping tango rhythm) while a bandoneon breathes the lead line, seductive and slow, as if the deal is a dance the mark is led through. Card shuffles and a soft click of a counter bell are woven into the rhythm. At the switch the bandoneon hits one hard sforzando stab with a staccato piano cluster, then everything stops. From 10.5 s only a bandoneon sustains a single quiet, unresolved note over a curtain swish, leaving the space open. Instrumental, invented melody, no ragtime.

name: cartoon-studio-mickey-mouse-cue
idea: A 1930s studio cartoon orchestra scoring every movement on the cards, Carl Stalling style: a tiptoeing bassoon is the lead voice for the dealer, pizzicato strings and a wood block tick through the dithering pick, and a xylophone run and slide whistle do the envelope fan. The switch lands on a bright brass stinger chord with a cymbal crash, as if the trick were a joke. Then at 10.5 s the comedy drains away: a low muffled timpani roll fades to near silence under one held cello note, and a heavy curtain pulls. Instrumental, quick and slapstick, then suddenly serious.
